I am 56 years old, and I have worked this land for 30 years. I never went to school, but I learned from my mother, my husband, and from watching the crops and the sky every season. My household has six people, and some of my children work in the city, so I do not have endless labor at home. That is why I must be practical.

My 10.9 mu cannot all go to cotton, even if the price is sometimes good—cotton needs too much hand-picking, and my hands are not as strong as they were twenty years ago. So I will keep 8 mu in my wheat-maize double crop. That is our foundation. It feeds us, it is familiar, and I can manage it with the help of my husband and our well. The wheat is already in the ground from last autumn. Now that it is greening up, I will top-dress urea when the soil is moist enough, and I will irrigate three times: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I do not irrigate more than that because pumping costs money, and I have learned that too much water makes the wheat lodge. I will spray pesticide twice when I see aphids or rust starting.

After wheat harvest in early June, there is barely two weeks before I must plant maize. I will not waste time ploughing; I will sow hybrid maize seed directly into the stubble. Time is more valuable than perfect tilth in that gap. I will apply fertilizer at sowing and again at the big trumpet stage, and irrigate twice—once if the June heat is cruel, and again at silking. I know this field well; 550 kg/mu is a realistic hope if the rains do not fail completely.

The remaining 2.9 mu I will plant cotton in late April. Cotton gives cash, which we need for my grandchildren’s school costs. My daughter-in-law will help with the picking in autumn. I will rotary-till that plot, lay down compound fertilizer, and plant an improved variety I have saved seed from before—I do not trust every new seed salesman who comes to the village. Cotton attracts bollworms without fail, so I will spray four times. I will irrigate three times, especially when the bolls are setting. I expect about 90 kg/mu of seed cotton. I keep my nitrogen and pesticide use moderate. I have seen neighbors spend too much on inputs and end the year with empty pockets. Experience has taught me that steady, careful management brings more profit than gambling on maximum yields.
